title: The Remains of the Day
wiki_lead:
The Remains of the Day is a 1989 novel by the Nobel Prize-winning British author Kazuo Ishiguro. The protagonist, Stevens, is a butler with a long record of service at Darlington Hall, a fictitious stately home near Oxford, England. In 1956, he takes a motoring holiday to visit a former colleague, and reminisces about events at Darlington Hall in the 1920s and 1930s.
The work won the Booker Prize for Fiction in 1989. A film adaptation of the novel, made in 1993 and starring Anthony Hopkins and Emma Thompson, was nominated for eight Academy Awards. In 2022, it was included on the "Big Jubilee Read" list of 70 books by Commonwealth authors, selected to celebrate the Platinum Jubilee of Elizabeth II.

Plot
In 1956, Stevens, the narrator, is butler at Darlington Hall, a position he held for decades under the Hall's previous owner, Lord Darlington. After Darlington's death, the Hall was purchased by a wealthy American, Mr Farraday, who kept Stevens on, although with a much reduced staff. Stevens frets that he is unable to maintain professional standards, and when he receives a letter from a former colleague, the ex-housekeeper Mrs Benn (née Kenton), he detects hints that she has left her husband and that although many years have passed she might be interested in resuming her old position. Mr Farraday encourages Stevens to take a holiday, offering to lend him a car. Stevens accepts, and sets out for Cornwall where Mrs Benn now lives.
The novel intertwines the events of the next few days, as Stevens motors down to Cornwall, with memories of his professional life under Lord Darlington. He recalls his unswerving determination to meet his profession's highest standards of dignity, his unshakable loyalty, and his pride in having served an important gentleman doing great things in international affairs. He recalls early disagreements with Miss Kenton over professional procedures when she first joined the staff in 1922, followed by a growing respect over the subsequent years. He recalls Miss Kenton making occasional personal overtures, such as bringing flowers to brighten up his pantry, but reminds himself that he always remained professional, refusing to let such matters interfere with the dignity he considered his position required. 
Stevens recollects that as an honest English gentleman Lord Darlington had felt it morally right after the war to bring Germany back into the 'civilised world', and that he had worked tirelessly to mitigate the worst effects of the Treaty of Versailles. The Hall became a regular meeting place for like-minded gentlemen of many nationalities. On one occasion, Stevens had facilitated an important secret meeting involving the Prime Minister and the German ambassador, Herr Ribbentrop. That evening, Miss Kenton had attempted to speak to Stevens concerning a proposal of marriage she had received, evidently expecting some personal response, but Stevens had brushed her off and remained focused on his duties. grok_lead: The Remains of the Day is a 1989 novel by Kazuo Ishiguro, narrated in the first person by Stevens, the head butler of Darlington Hall, who embarks on a motoring trip across England's West Country in July 1956 and reflects on his decades of service to his former employer, Lord Darlington, during the interwar period. The narrative unfolds through Stevens's reminiscences, which reveal his rigid adherence to professional dignity and loyalty, even as they expose his emotional repression and the personal costs of his devotion to duty over individual fulfillment. Key themes include the nature of service and self-sacrifice, the unreliability of memory, and the quiet regrets arising from unspoken affections and moral blindness, particularly Stevens's unwavering support for Lord Darlington's pro-appeasement efforts toward Nazi Germany in the 1930s. The novel received widespread critical acclaim for its subtle exploration of English national identity and the psychological toll of unquestioned loyalty, culminating in Ishiguro's win of the Booker Prize in 1989, selected from a shortlist that included works by Margaret Atwood and John Irving. Judges praised its "profoundly moving" portrayal of a man confronting the "remains" of his life, highlighting Ishiguro's mastery of restrained prose and unreliable narration that invites readers to discern truths Stevens himself suppresses. Adapted into a 1993 film directed by James Ivory starring Anthony Hopkins as Stevens and Emma Thompson as the housekeeper Miss Kenton, the work has endured as a cornerstone of Ishiguro's oeuvre, contributing to his 2017 Nobel Prize in Literature for novels that "uncover the abyss beneath our illusory sense of connection with the world." While some critics have noted its unflinching depiction of complicity in historical moral failures without overt judgment, the book avoids didacticism, instead emphasizing personal introspection over political polemic.
